title: The Sheaf and the Eighty Designs: Kingston, the Green Sheaf, 291, and the Unmarked Grave at Bude
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Crossings: Pimlico, Kingston, and the Annancy Tellers

stops.name: 28 Belgrave Road, Pimlico: the birth
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Date from Wikipedia; the address 28 Belgrave Road is given directly by Kaplan, Encyclopedia of Tarot III, so the earlier caution that the street number was Wikipedia-only is dropped. No birth certificate has been reproduced in any source consulted. Coordinate derived from the OSM position of 25 Belgrave Road, SW1V; the individual house is not pinned. The twenty-five crossings figure is Smith's own contemporary claim and is [R].
stops.campa: At 28 Belgrave Road in Pimlico, an American couple resident in London have a daughter and name her Pamela Colman Smith. The house is rented. Charles Edward Smith is a merchant whose work keeps the household moving between Britain, New England, and the Caribbean; Corinne Colman comes from a family of painters. Their daughter's first decade is arrivals and departures with a trunk, Manchester and New England and the islands. She will tell an interviewer later that she crossed the Atlantic twenty-five times before she was twenty-two.
suggested_refs: 28 Belgrave Road, Pimlico, the London house of an American merchant family
Bryn Mawr College Special Collections, Smith's letters of 1896-1900 to her cousin Mary B. Reed
sources: Stuart R. Kaplan, The Encyclopedia of Tarot, Volume III (1990)

stops.name: Kingston, the household moves to Jamaica
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the move and its stated cause (Wikipedia; 1890s.ca). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. No family address in Kingston survives in the sources consulted, so the coordinate is the city pin. The quote is from the book she published ten years later in New York, not from a Jamaican manuscript; it is placed here because the material is Jamaican.
stops.campa: Charles Edward Smith takes a post connected to the West India Improvement Company and the household moves to Kingston. Pamela is eleven. What the island teaches her is on no curriculum: the Annancy cycle, the spider who wins every contest by talking, carried in the Creole of the people who tell it, with the song and the gesture and the timed pause that belong to the telling. She learns the stories as performance before she learns them as text. Ten years later she will set them down in New York, spelling the speech the way she heard it.
stops.quote: IN a long before time in dis country dere lib Chim-chim Bird, and Chim-chim Bird him buil' him nest on de top of de grass; so dat it blow up an' down wid de wind.
stops.quote_source: Pamela Colman Smith, Annancy Stories (New York: R. H. Russell, 1899), opening lines of 'Annancy and Chim-Chim', p. 9; Internet Archive, identifier cu31924079620021
suggested_refs: Annancy Stories (R. H. Russell, 1899), the Jamaican cycle as she set it down

stops.name: Kingston, the toy theatre and the buccaneer
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 1896 Kingston staging of 'Henry Morgan' is a later reconstruction, not a contemporaneous record. Mary K. Greer documents Smith's toy-theatre performances at a Brooklyn fair in December 1897 but does not confirm a Kingston production in 1896, so both date and venue are traditional. Month and day defaulted to 01. Kingston city pin.
stops.campa: She builds theatres the size of a table and works them herself: painted flats, hundreds of cut figures, the penny plain and tuppence coloured trade of London reassembled on a Caribbean verandah. Tradition gives her a production of Henry Morgan, the buccaneer who sacked Panama and died governing this island, staged with elaborate scenery for whoever will sit and watch. She speaks all the parts in the voices she has learned from the tellers, so the bogey of the Annancy tales walks straight into the toy proscenium with his bag over his shoulder.
stops.quote: if you lie, or tell fib, Missa Titman he gwine come an' catch you an' put you in him bag, an' den him will corn you, an' h'eat you!
stops.quote_source: Pamela Colman Smith, Annancy Stories (New York: R. H. Russell, 1899), closing line of 'Mr. Titman', p. 20
suggested_refs: The English toy-theatre trade, penny plain and twopence coloured, as she rebuilt it in Kingston

stops.name: Kingston, the mother's death
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year (Wikipedia; corroborated by the research pool). No month, day, or burial place is recorded in anything consulted; date defaulted to 1896-01-01. The Bryn Mawr finding aid for the Mary B. Reed correspondence returned HTTP 403 in this pass, so its 1896-1900 range and the addressee are taken from the pool and not re-verified.
stops.campa: Corinne Colman Smith dies in Jamaica. Her daughter is eighteen and enrolled at an art school in Brooklyn, and is now without the parent who came from the painting family. The letters Pamela writes in these years to her cousin Mary B. Reed survive at Bryn Mawr and carry the shape of the break in them: schooling interrupted, money uncertain, a household reduced to a father whose work keeps moving. Three years later he dies too. Where either of them was buried is not recorded in anything that has been printed.
suggested_refs: Bryn Mawr College Special Collections, BMC-M47, Smith's outgoing letters 1896-1900
sources: Bryn Mawr College Special Collections finding aid (inaccessible, HTTP 403)

segments.name: Pratt Institute, and the Trade of Illustration

stops.name: Pratt Institute, Willoughby Avenue: the training under Dow
stops.date_confidence: Attested: enrollment c. 1893 at about fifteen, study under Arthur Wesley Dow, confirmed by Wikipedia and by Pratt's own press page. Exact enrollment month not recorded; September assumed for the academic year and should be read as approximate. Coordinate corrected to OSM 'Pratt Institute, 200 Willoughby Avenue' (40.69134, -73.96302); the figure in the research pool sat 245 m north, across the avenue.
stops.campa: At about fifteen she enrolls at Pratt Institute on Willoughby Avenue and falls under Arthur Wesley Dow, who is rebuilding American art teaching around line, notan, and colour. Dow does not set his students to copying casts. He sets them to filling a rectangle: flat pattern held in balance, the Japanese print read as a diagram of decisions already made. Notan, the middle term, is the weighing of the dark mass against the light one before any subject is chosen. She studies under him for about four years.
suggested_refs: Arthur Wesley Dow, Composition (1899), the method as he published it
sources: Pratt Institute, 'Overlooked No More: Pamela Colman Smith'

stops.name: Brooklyn, leaving Pratt without a diploma
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year and to the reported reason (illness), per Wikipedia. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. The nature of the illness is not named in any source consulted and is left as a gap.
stops.campa: She leaves Pratt in 1897 without taking a degree, the reason reported as illness. No account then or since has named what the illness was. She is nineteen and already earning: illustrated ballad sheets, Christmas cards, hand-coloured prints of scenes from Shakespeare, work made to be sold rather than shown. The letters that survive between her father, herself, and the dealer William Macbeth turn on consignments and prices, not on ambition or on schools.
suggested_refs: Pratt Institute records of the 1893-1897 cohort

stops.name: Macbeth Gallery, Fifth Avenue: the prints sell
stops.date_confidence: Attested that her work sold regularly through the Macbeth Gallery on Fifth Avenue by the end of 1897 (Kaplan, quoting letters from Smith and her father to William Macbeth). [R] on any exhibition: no one-person show is documented in Kaplan, in Wikipedia's Macbeth Gallery article, or in the Mary K. Greer post cited for it, and the widely repeated 'first exhibition' framing is not carried here. The 237 Fifth Avenue street number is [R] and is confirmed by neither; the coordinate corresponds to that number if it is right.
stops.campa: By the end of 1897 her work is selling steadily through William Macbeth's gallery on Fifth Avenue: ballad sheets, Christmas cards, hand-coloured prints of Shakespearean scenes. Macbeth is the dealer who backs American artists in a market that would rather buy Europe, and the arrangement with Smith is a standing account rather than an occasion. Later writers give her a first exhibition in these rooms. No catalogue, no notice, and no letter about such a show has ever been produced.
suggested_refs: Macbeth Gallery papers, Archives of American Art, for the Smith consignments

stops.name: R. H. Russell, New York: Annancy Stories published
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the book itself, New York, R. H. Russell, 1899, seen in the Internet Archive scan cu31924079620021. Month unrecorded, defaulted to 01. The publisher's Union Square area address is approximate and not independently confirmed. The father's death in 1899 is attested by Wikipedia, which does not specify the place; it is folded into this stop rather than pinned to a location the sources do not give.
stops.campa: R. H. Russell publishes Annancy Stories, her first book, written and illustrated by her, the Jamaican cycle set down in the Creole she heard it in with her own drawings around it. The publisher's front matter explains her to New York as a young lady lately come from Jamaica and measures her against Uncle Remus. She is twenty-one. Her father dies the same year, and she is left with no parents, one book, and the beginnings of a name in the New York trade. Before the year is out she sails for England.
stops.quote: The "Annancy Stories," by Miss Pamela Colman Smith, a young lady who has recently come from Jamaica to live in this country, are perhaps the most original contribution to negro folk-lore literature since the day when "Uncle Remus" gave us his imperishable record of "Brer Rabbit."
stops.quote_source: Unsigned publisher's introduction, Annancy Stories (New York: R. H. Russell, 1899), p. [iii]
suggested_refs: Annancy Stories (1899), full scan, Internet Archive cu31924079620021

segments.name: London: the Lyceum, the Studio, the Temple

stops.name: Lyceum Theatre, Wellington Street: the theatrical household
stops.date_confidence: Attested that she returned to England in 1899, the year her father died (Wikipedia), and that she worked in and around the Lyceum circle (1890s.ca). [R] on regular salaried employment at the theatre, which 1890s.ca explicitly declines to establish; intermittent design, illustration, companionship, and touring is the supported form. [R] on the nickname Pixie and its attribution to Ellen Terry: repeated everywhere, attested nowhere fetched. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: She returns to England in the year her father dies and attaches herself to the household around the Lyceum: Ellen Terry, Henry Irving, and their business manager Bram Stoker. She draws actors in role, designs theatrical matter, travels with or near the company. Whether she is ever on the payroll is unrecorded; what the accounts support is intermittent work, design and illustration and the companionship of a useful friend with a pen. The name Pixie is said to come from Terry, and it is what she will be called for the rest of her life. Nobody has traced the saying to its source.
suggested_refs: Smallhythe Place, Tenterden, Ellen Terry's house and its theatre, suffrage, and Smith-related holdings; no dated visit by Smith is attested

stops.name: Milborne Grove, The Boltons: the studio and the weekly open house
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year: Wikipedia has her establishing a studio in London in 1901 and holding a weekly open house. The research pool conflated this with her 1899 return under a single 1901 date; the two are separated here. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected to OSM Milborne Grove (51.48717, -0.18092). Her 1901 visitors' book gives 13 Milborne Grove and the Green Sheaf colophon gives 14; both are recorded, neither adjudicated. The locality is The Boltons, in Kensington and Chelsea, usually called South Kensington rather than Chelsea.
stops.campa: In 1901 she takes a studio in London and opens it once a week to anyone in the arts who cares to come: painters, writers, actors, occultists, the London wing of the Irish revival. She reads the Annancy stories aloud in the voices, in costume, to rooms of Londoners who have never heard anything like it. Her visitors' book that year gives her address as 13 Milborne Grove; the magazine she starts two years later gives 14. They are the same short street off The Boltons, and nobody has explained the discrepancy.
suggested_refs: Smith's 1901 visitors' book, quoted in Kaplan, Encyclopedia of Tarot III

stops.name: Isis-Urania Temple, London: the initiation
stops.date_confidence: November 1901 per Wikipedia. The introduction by W. B. Yeats is [R]: universally repeated, not independently attested in anything fetched, though Yeats's own initiation into Isis-Urania on 7 March 1890 at Mark Masons' Hall is attested in his file. Her grade history is not consistently recorded anywhere consulted, so her passage through the Adeptus Minor ceremony is inferred from the Order's general practice and is not attested for her. Coordinate marks central London only: no 1901 meeting address for Isis-Urania was confirmed. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: She is initiated into the Isis-Urania Temple of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, brought in, the tradition holds, by W. B. Yeats, who has been in the Order eleven years. The charter the Order works is Rosicrucian: its inner grade seats the candidate in a built replica of the seven-sided vault of Christian Rosenkreuz, opened after a hundred and twenty years with the body uncorrupted inside it. She joins in the middle of the Order's worst year. No grade certificate of hers has ever been found.
suggested_refs: The Adeptus Minor ceremony of the Golden Dawn and its built vault, as described in the Order's own rituals
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn'

stops.name: Vigo Street, London: A Broad Sheet, coloured by hand
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The collaboration with Jack B. Yeats on A Broad Sheet in 1902 comes from the research pool by way of tradition and was not independently confirmed by any source fetched in this pass. Issue-level attribution between the two artists is explicitly flagged in the pool as unchecked. Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate is Elkin Mathews's Vigo Street shop, the London counter for the sheet, not a workshop address.
stops.campa: With Jack B. Yeats she makes A Broad Sheet, a monthly folio of ballads and pictures, printed plain and then coloured a sheet at a time, in editions small enough that colouring them at all is possible. Which of the two artists made which plates, in which issue, has never been worked out. No process block, no half-tone: the colour goes on after the press, by a person holding a brush. She will build her own magazine on the same method the following year, and it will hold the edition down the same way.
suggested_refs: A Broad Sheet (1902-1903), surviving hand-coloured runs
sources: Research pool, tradition (not independently confirmed by a fetched source)

stops.name: London, the Order breaks and Waite founds a rite
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the 1903 schism and Waite's founding of the Independent and Rectified Order R.R. et A.C. (Wikipedia, 'Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn' and 'Arthur Edward Waite'). Smith's own membership in the rite, and its duration of roughly four years, come from the research pool and were not re-verified against a fetched primary source, so the Smith side is [R]. Waite's own file gives the rite's founding location as uncertain between London and Geneva; the London pin is used here because Smith is in London. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Golden Dawn comes apart. Waite and Blackden keep the Isis-Urania name, Felkin's people leave as Stella Matutina, and the quarrel that produced this has been running since Mathers initiated Crowley in Paris and W. B. Yeats printed, at his own cost, a pamphlet asking whether the Order intended to remain a magical order at all. Smith follows Arthur Edward Waite into the Independent and Rectified Order R.R. et A.C., an inward Christian mysticism with the ceremonial magic taken out of it. She stays about four years.
suggested_refs: W. B. Yeats, 'Is the Order of R.R. et A.C. to Remain a Magical Order?' (privately printed, 1901)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn'

stops.name: 14 Milborne Grove: the Green Sheaf begins
stops.date_confidence: Attested: thirteen issues from May 1903 to May 1904, edited, published, hand-coloured, and sold by Smith herself (Wikipedia; 1890s.ca; Boston College Burns Library). The colophon address 14 Milborne Grove, The Boltons, S.W. is quoted directly in Kaplan from the magazine's own pages. Coordinate corrected to OSM Milborne Grove. Day defaulted to 01 within the attested month.
stops.campa: She starts a magazine and does all of it herself: edits it, publishes it, prints it on hand-made paper, colours every plate by hand, sells it from her own front door. The Green Sheaf runs thirteen issues in a year and carries work by Yeats, Gordon Craig, John Masefield, Cecil French, and Smith. The colophon names no publishing house at all, only an editor and a street number: 14 Milborne Grove, The Boltons, S.W. She is twenty-five when the first issue goes out in May.
stops.quote: My Sheaf is small . . . but it is green. I will gather into my Sheaf all the young fresh things I can—pictures, verses, ballads of love and war; tales of pirates and the sea.
stops.quote_source: The Green Sheaf, No. I (London, 1903), unsigned editorial prospectus, first text page; Internet Archive, identifier green-sheaf
suggested_refs: The Green Sheaf, complete run of thirteen issues, Internet Archive identifier green-sheaf
sources: The Green Sheaf No. I (1903), Internet Archive green-sheaf

stops.name: Elkin Mathews, Vigo Street: the London counter
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Elkin Mathews's Vigo Street shop was one of the London outlets for The Green Sheaf during its thirteen-issue run (1890s.ca, confirmed by fetch). The John Baillie exhibition and the reciprocal advertising arrangement come from the pool and are [R] as to the Baker Street address, which was not independently re-confirmed. Month chosen to sit inside the run; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Sheaf is sold through Elkin Mathews's shop in Vigo Street, publisher to the Yellow Book poets and the natural counter in London for a hand-coloured folio. John Baillie shows her watercolours at his gallery in Baker Street and takes advertising space in her pages in exchange. The arrangement is barter, and the margins are thin. Each copy costs her the hours she spends laying the colour on, so the size of the run is set by how many hours there are.
stops.quote: Ripe ears are good for bread, but green ears are good for pleasure.
stops.quote_source: The Green Sheaf, No. I (London, 1903), editorial prospectus; Internet Archive, identifier green-sheaf
suggested_refs: Elkin Mathews's Vigo Street list, 1903-1904

stops.name: Brentano's, Union Square: the Sheaf reaches New York
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Brentano's carried The Green Sheaf in New York from the seventh issue onward (1890s.ca, confirmed by fetch). The seventh issue's month is not stated in the sources consulted; November 1903 is an estimate placed inside the attested May 1903 to May 1904 run and should be read as ordering, not as a date. Brentano's Union Square coordinate is approximate.
stops.campa: From the seventh issue Brentano's on Union Square carries The Green Sheaf, and a folio coloured by hand in South Kensington has an American counter. Smith knows the city: she was selling prints through Macbeth on Fifth Avenue six years earlier, and her first book came out of a New York house. How many copies Brentano's moved is not recorded, and neither is what she was paid for them. She has kept an outlet on both sides of the Atlantic since she was nineteen years old.
stops.quote: You will find ballads of the old world in my Sheaf. Are they not green for ever . . .
stops.quote_source: The Green Sheaf, No. I (London, 1903), editorial prospectus; Internet Archive, identifier green-sheaf
suggested_refs: Brentano's Union Square store, American outlet for The Green Sheaf

stops.name: Park Mansions Arcade, Knightsbridge: the shop and the school of hand-colouring
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Kaplan quotes the magazine's own announcement placing the shop at Park Mansions Arcade, Knightsbridge, and the Boston College Burns Library blog dates it to the twelfth issue, 1904, specifying that it was the Green Sheaf School of Hand-Colouring's shop. The pool's claim that no precise address survives is wrong and is corrected here. Park Mansions Arcade fronts Brompton Road opposite Harrods; coordinate set accordingly rather than at the district centroid. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: By the twelfth issue there is a shop. The Green Sheaf School of Hand-Colouring takes premises at Park Mansions Arcade in Knightsbridge, opposite Harrods, selling the Press's books, prints, stationery, bookplates, and lessons in the colouring itself, with commercial illustration taken to order. Smith is editor, publisher, printer, colourist, shopkeeper, and teacher of the craft, all of it at once and all of it out of one pair of hands. One issue of the magazine is left to run.
stops.quote: O deary me how idle is / This great and weary town. / For people talk and never do / As they go up and down.
stops.quote_source: 'The Town,' signed P.C.S., The Green Sheaf, Vol. XII (London, 1904), p. 136; Internet Archive, identifier green-sheaf
suggested_refs: Park Mansions Arcade, Brompton Road, Knightsbridge, premises of the Green Sheaf School of Hand-Colouring
sources: Boston College John J. Burns Library blog, 'The Many Business Endeavors of Pamela Colman Smith'
The Green Sheaf Vol. XII (1904), Internet Archive green-sheaf

stops.name: London, the Green Sheaf Press outlives the magazine
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the Green Sheaf Press was established around 1904 and published books, primarily by women writers, operating until at least 1906 (Wikipedia). The magazine's last issue is May 1904, so June 1904 is used to order the Press after it; the founding month is not recorded. A complete list of Green Sheaf Press titles was not located in any source consulted and is recorded here as an open gap.
stops.campa: The magazine stops after thirteen issues and the press outlives it. The Green Sheaf Press publishes books, most of them by women, at least as late as 1906. She is twenty-six and running a complete small publishing house out of her own labour and a South Kensington address, at an age when most of her contemporaries are still hunting a first commission. It never turns a profit. No list of its titles has been established, and no record of a winding-up survives in the sources consulted; the imprint simply stops appearing.
stops.quote: I hope you will have my Sheaf in your house and like it. It will stay fresh and green then.
stops.quote_source: The Green Sheaf, No. I (London, 1903), editorial prospectus; Internet Archive, identifier green-sheaf
suggested_refs: Green Sheaf Press imprints, 1904-1906; no complete list has been established
sources: Boston College John J. Burns Library blog, 'The Many Business Endeavors of Pamela Colman Smith'

segments.name: 291, and the Pictures Made to Music

stops.name: London, painting to music
stops.date_confidence: The three surviving music pictures at the Tate are all dated 1907 by the museum; the practice itself is undated in the sources consulted. June 1906 is used only to place the working method before the January 1907 New York exhibition and should not be read as a date. Studio coordinate is her Milborne Grove pin, which is where she is known to have worked in this period; no source names the room the music pictures were made in.
stops.campa: She paints while music is played, working fast in watercolour to whatever is on the piano, and calls the results her music pictures: a Grieg spring song, a Sinding impromptu, Mozart's Prague symphony. She does not offer them as illustrations of the pieces, and nobody who watched her work described what she thought she was doing. Three survive, at the Tate, all dated 1907. When the practice began is not recorded anywhere consulted. It is this work Alfred Stieglitz will hang in New York in January.
suggested_refs: Tate, 'Grieg: Spring Song', 'Impromptu (Sinding)', and 'Mozart: Symphony Prague', all 1907
sources: Tate, artist page for Pamela Colman Smith

stops.name: 291 Fifth Avenue, the first exhibition at the Little Galleries
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Run of 5 to 22 January 1907 and the eight-day extension from Kaplan, who also gives roughly 2,200 visitors, more than any previous photography show in the rooms. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: Wikipedia's 'Alfred Stieglitz' article says all of her exhibited works were sold, while Kaplan quotes the Photo-Secession's own report of thirty-three drawings sold and Wikipedia's '291 (art gallery)' article says only that a substantial number sold; the outlier is the Stieglitz article. The often-repeated count of seventy-two exhibited works appears in none of the sources consulted and is not carried. Coordinate from Wikipedia's '291 (art gallery)' article; Kaplan's text calls the gallery 'Madison Avenue', which is an error in Kaplan.
stops.campa: Alfred Stieglitz gives the Little Galleries of the Photo-Secession over to drawings and watercolours, the first time those rooms have shown anything that is not a photograph. The exhibition runs from the fifth to the twenty-second of January, is held over another eight days, and draws some two thousand two hundred people, more than any photography show he has put on there. Thirty-three of the drawings go into New York collections. Stieglitz makes a platinum-print portfolio of twenty-two of her paintings.
suggested_refs: Stieglitz's platinum-print portfolio of twenty-two Smith paintings, 1907

stops.name: 291 Fifth Avenue, the return exhibitions
stops.date_confidence: Second show 26 February to 11 March 1908 per Kaplan; a third showing in 1909 is attested by Wikipedia without dates and is folded into this stop rather than given a date the sources do not supply. The number of her works remaining in the Stieglitz collection could not be checked: archives.yale.edu returned HTTP 403 in this pass, so the figure of eleven works on paper given in the research pool is [R] and is not stated here.
stops.campa: Stieglitz shows her a second time in the spring of 1908 and a third time in 1909. The 1909 showing is attested without dates; no source consulted gives the month it opened or how long it stayed up. She is the artist who opened his gallery to something other than photography, and she keeps her place in it. None of it makes her solvent. What does not sell stays with Stieglitz; it sits now in the Stieglitz and O'Keeffe archive at Yale, catalogued with her letters to him about money.
suggested_refs: Alfred Stieglitz / Georgia O'Keeffe Archive, Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, for the Smith correspondence and works on paper

stops.name: Pratt Institute Assembly Hall, Ryerson Street: the Magic Spectacles lecture
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Mary K. Greer gives the lecture as Tuesday night, 23 March 1909, in the Assembly Hall of Pratt Institute on Ryerson Street, reported in a newspaper account of Thursday 25 March. The research pool carried the report date as the event date; the correction is followed here. The dress description is confirmed verbatim in Greer. Coordinate approximate along Ryerson Street at Pratt.
stops.campa: She comes back to Pratt as a speaker and gives a lecture called Magic Spectacles in the Assembly Hall on Ryerson Street, on a Tuesday night, to an audience drawn from Brooklyn and Manhattan both. She is thirty-one. She enrolled here at fifteen, lately off a boat from Kingston, and left without a diploma. A reporter writes her down in detail: pussy-willow gray, a high-crowned gray hat with a box pleating of bottle-green ribbon on it, coal-black curly hair underneath.
suggested_refs: The Brooklyn newspaper account of 25 March 1909, quoted in Mary K. Greer, 'Pamela Colman Smith 1909: Magic Spectacles'
sources: Mary K. Greer, 'Pamela Colman Smith 1909: Magic Spectacles'

stops.name: London, the letter of 19 November
stops.date_confidence: 19 November 1909, not 18: Kaplan quotes the letter, and the research pool's geography and chronology entries were two views of one document carrying two different dates. The letter is written from London and held in the Alfred Stieglitz / Georgia O'Keeffe Archive at Yale; the pool's placement of it at the gallery coordinate is corrected. The primary manuscript could not be fetched in this pass (Yale archives HTTP 403), so the wording follows Kaplan's transcription.
stops.campa: She writes to Stieglitz from London to ask whether a buyer's money for The Moon has come in, and whether he can send it, because she wants some money for Christmas. Then, in the same paragraph, she mentions the job she has just finished. It is the only account of the tarot commission in her own hand that anyone has found, and it runs to one sentence, thrown in after the request for the money. The rest of the page is about the debt. The deck will not be printed for another month.
stops.quote: I've just finished a big job for very little cash! a set of designs for a pack of Tarot cards 80 designs
stops.quote_source: Smith to Alfred Stieglitz, 19 November 1909, Alfred Stieglitz / Georgia O'Keeffe Archive, Beinecke Library, Yale; quoted in Kaplan, Encyclopedia of Tarot III
suggested_refs: The 19 November 1909 Stieglitz letter, Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University
sources: Mary K. Greer, 'Pamela Colman Smith 1909: Magic Spectacles'

stops.name: London, the commission from Waite
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Waite commissioned the deck and that the designs were made in 1909; the April to October span comes from Waite's own file and the research pool. No contract, fee figure, royalty clause, or copyright assignment for Smith's designs has ever surfaced, so 'flat fee' rests on her own phrase 'very little cash' and on the absence of any later payment. [R]: the claim that she worked from the Sola Busca photographs deposited at the British Museum in 1907 rests on real visual parallels in the Three of Swords and Ten of Wands, but no record places her in front of them, and the 1907 deposit itself was not independently confirmed in this pass. Coordinate is the central London pin used for the direction sessions in Waite's own file; where they actually worked is unrecorded. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Arthur Edward Waite, whose rite she has belonged to since 1903, commissions a complete tarot from her and specifies the symbolism card by card. She draws all seventy-eight between about April and October, in six months, for a flat fee. The twenty-two trumps follow his programme closely. The fifty-six minor cards, which no earlier printed deck had drawn as scenes at all, are largely her own invention: figures out in weather, on roads, at tables, doing things. She signs each of the seventy-eight with her initials, a small monogram tucked into a corner of the picture.
suggested_refs: The Sola Busca tarot photographs deposited at the British Museum, cited for the visual parallels in the Three of Swords and Ten of Wands; no record places Smith in front of them

stops.name: 164 Aldersgate Street, London: Rider publishes the deck
stops.date_confidence: Attested: December 1909 publication by William Rider & Son with Waite's The Key to the Tarot, the maroon box and the roses-and-lilies backs, the halt of the first run around April 1910 over cardstock, the free upgrade offered to buyers, and five known surviving copies of the true first edition (wopc.co.uk; Wikipedia, 'Rider-Waite tarot deck'). Coordinate inherited byte-identical from arthur_edward_waite.journey.json. The research pool's alternative Paternoster Row placement is an error and is not used: the deck's own 1909 imprint reads 164 Aldersgate Street. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: William Rider and Son bring the deck out from 164 Aldersgate Street in December 1909, in a maroon box, the backs printed with roses and lilies, together with Waite's small guide The Key to the Tarot. The cardstock fails. The run is halted around April 1910, buyers are offered a free upgrade to the second edition, and five copies of that true first edition are known to survive. The chromolithographic plates will be destroyed in the next war, so every edition after that descends from printed cards rather than from her drawings.
suggested_refs: The 1909 Rider imprint, 'William Rider & Sons Limited, 164 Aldersgate Street, London E.C.'

stops.name: London, the Suffrage Atelier
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Smith was a member of the Suffrage Atelier (1890s.ca; Wikipedia, 'Suffrage Atelier', which lists her among members). Founders corrected to Laurence Housman, Clemence Housman, and Alfred Pearse, February 1909; the pool omitted Pearse. [R] on the coordinate: no premises address for the Atelier was found in any source consulted, and the point is a west London placeholder. [R] on the date: her period of activity is given loosely as c. 1909-1914 and 1910 is an ordering choice. Her individual output for the Atelier cannot be inventoried, since its production records are incomplete.
stops.campa: She joins the Suffrage Atelier, founded the previous year by Laurence Housman, Clemence Housman, and Alfred Pearse to make propaganda for the women's vote: posters, handbills, banners, printed cheap and fast by the artists themselves. It is the method of her own magazine turned to a campaign, minus the colouring by hand. Smith is on the membership rolls. What she made for it cannot be listed, because the Atelier kept incomplete production records and most of its work went out unsigned.
suggested_refs: Suffrage Atelier prints and banners, 1909-1914, mostly unsigned

stops.name: London, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the 1911 revision and expansion of Waite's guide as The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, illustrating all seventy-eight cards and crediting the designs to Pamela Colman Smith (Wikipedia, 'Rider-Waite tarot deck'). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. The American copyright lapse in 1966 is attested in the same article's copyright section. [R]: the claim that Rider reissued the deck through 1939 and again from 1971 to 1977 carries a citation-needed tag on Wikipedia dated January 2025 and is not stated here as fact.
stops.campa: Waite's guide is revised and enlarged as The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, printing all seventy-eight cards and naming the designs as Pamela Colman Smith's. The credit is there in the text, from the first edition. Whether Rider chose the trade name or Waite did is not recorded in anything consulted. What is on the box is Rider Waite, the publisher and the author, and a reader who never opens the guide has no reason to learn there was a third person in the room.
suggested_refs: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (London: William Rider & Son, 1911)

stops.name: Farm Street, Mayfair: received into the Church
stops.date_confidence: Attested on Smith's own testimony: her entry in the Catholic Who's Who for 1939, quoted verbatim in Kaplan, reads 'Rec'd into the Church at Farm Street 1911; Parc Garland, The Lizard, Cornwall.' Farm Street is the Jesuit church of the Immaculate Conception, Mayfair. Contradiction flagged: 1890s.ca states that she converted during a New York residence of roughly 1911-1914. Her own entry names a London church and a year, and is preferred here; the New York reading is recorded, not adopted. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: She is received into the Roman Catholic Church at Farm Street, the Jesuit church of the Immaculate Conception in Mayfair. The fact comes from her own hand: her entry in the Catholic Who's Who for 1939 gives the year and the church by name. It is the same year The Pictorial Key appears with her designs in it. She is thirty-three, and will be a Catholic for the remaining forty years of her life. One account puts the conversion in New York instead, some years later; her own entry names a London church and a year.
suggested_refs: Smith's entry in the Catholic Who's Who, 1939, quoted in Kaplan, Encyclopedia of Tarot III
sources: 1890s.ca, 'Pamela Colman Smith: a biography' (dissenting on place and date)

stops.name: London, illustrating The Lair of the White Worm
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Smith illustrated Bram Stoker's last novel, published 1911 (Wikipedia). Coordinate is the central London pin: no source names where she worked in 1911, and her Milborne Grove tenure cannot be traced past the Green Sheaf years.
stops.campa: Bram Stoker, whom she has known since the Lyceum years, publishes his last novel and she illustrates it: a book about a woman who is a white worm living in a hole in the English ground, written by a man who is dying. The plates are hers, in colour, and unlike most of what she draws they carry her name where a reader will see it. It is the last commission the theatrical household sends her way. Irving died in 1905. Stoker dies in April of the year after this book.
suggested_refs: Bram Stoker, The Lair of the White Worm (London: William Rider & Son, 1911), with Smith's colour plates

stops.name: London, Ellen Terry's The Russian Ballet
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year (Wikipedia). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. What Smith published after 1913 could not be traced in any source consulted; the thinning of her commissions is visible in the absence of records rather than asserted by any of them, and is recorded here as a gap rather than a finding.
stops.campa: Ellen Terry writes a book about the Diaghilev company that has just taken London apart, and Smith illustrates it. It is the last of their collaborations to reach print, fourteen years after she first drew Terry in role. Terry has another quarter century to live and will go on working. After 1913 the commissions thin out, and what Smith published in the thirty-eight years left to her could not be traced in any source consulted. She is thirty-five.
suggested_refs: Ellen Terry, The Russian Ballet (1913), illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith

stops.name: London, the rite is disbanded
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Waite's Independent and Rectified Order R.R. et A.C. was disbanded in 1914 and that Waite then left the Golden Dawn tradition entirely (Wikipedia, 'Arthur Edward Waite'). Smith's own membership and its roughly four-year duration remain [R], as at the 1903 stop. Month and day defaulted to 01. Central London pin, as for the other Order stops: no meeting address survives.
stops.campa: Waite dissolves the Independent and Rectified Order R.R. et A.C., eleven years after founding it, and leaves the Golden Dawn tradition altogether. What Smith's membership amounted to after about 1907 is not established: no roll, no grade certificate, and no letter of hers on the subject has been found. The body she joined in 1903 is gone, and the temple she was initiated into in 1901 has already broken twice. The year is 1914, and Europe goes to war in August.
suggested_refs: Waite's departure from the Golden Dawn tradition, 1914

segments.name: Parc Garland, and the Long Retreat West

stops.name: Parc Garland, the Lizard: the lease at the end of England
stops.date_confidence: Corrected from the pool's '1920s'. Kaplan puts the uncle's death and the move 'shortly after the war' and records the Catholic church at Parc Garland commencing regular service in February 1919; artcornwall gives 1918 and names the uncle Theodore. She LEASED: Kaplan and Wikipedia both say lease, and the widely repeated claim that she bought the house is wrong. Coordinate is unverifiable: Parc Garland resolves in neither OSM nor Nominatim, the research pool gives two different points for it, and Kaplan's village-church context points to Lizard village rather than Predannack. Treat as hamlet precision at best. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: An inheritance said to come from an uncle named Theodore lets her lease a house at Parc Garland on the Lizard, the last land in England. She goes there after the war, with Nora Lake, and stays twenty years. She has stopped selling, and almost nothing she paints in those twenty years has been traced to a date or a buyer. It is about as far from Fifth Avenue and Vigo Street as a person can get without leaving the country: cliff, gorse, serpentine rock, a village with almost no Catholics in it.
suggested_refs: Parc Garland, Lizard, Cornwall; the property's later owners report paint traces in the attic and obelisk-like garden structures, read locally as evidence of continued occult practice. No eyewitness account supports that reading.
sources: artcornwall.org, Dawn G. Robinson, 'Pious Pixie: Pamela Colman Smith'

stops.name: Our Lady of the Lizard: the sacristan
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Kaplan records that the Catholic church commenced regular service in February 1919 after being moved from the other end of the village to a stone building at Parc Garland, and that Smith served as sacristan of Our Lady of The Lizard. Day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: Wikipedia places the priests' holiday home 'in a neighbouring house', while Kaplan says she used her own house as a vacation home for Catholic clergymen. Same unverifiable coordinate as the preceding stop.
stops.campa: The mission church is moved from the far end of the village into a stone building at Parc Garland, directly behind her house, and begins regular service in February 1919. She is its sacristan: she keeps the vessels, the linen, the candles, the keys. She calls the place her Cathedral. The sources disagree about the other house, whether the holiday home she ran for Catholic priests was her own or the one next door. Kaplan says hers, Wikipedia says the neighbour's, and no deed has been produced either way.
suggested_refs: Our Lady of The Lizard, the mission church at Parc Garland, in regular service from February 1919

stops.name: Kynance Cove, the Lizard: the ground of twenty years
stops.date_confidence: [R]. artcornwall names Kynance and Cadgwith among the coves of the peninsula Smith knew during her Parc Garland years, without describing any specific documented episode at either; this is local ground rather than an attested event. Date 1925 is an ordering choice within the 1919-1939 residence and carries no evidentiary weight. Cadgwith likewise corrected to 49.9879, -5.1804 and named in the campa rather than given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: Kynance and Cadgwith are the coves of her twenty Cornish years, serpentine stacks on the one side and a gig cove with pilchard cellars on the other, a few miles apart across the peninsula. She is in her forties and fifties, without a gallery, a magazine, or a publisher, living at the end of a road on a lease she can barely keep up. The local accounts name these coves as her walking ground and stop there. No particular day of hers is recorded at either, and no drawing is dated from either.
suggested_refs: Kynance Cove and Cadgwith, named in the Cornish accounts of Smith's Lizard years
sources: artcornwall.org, Dawn G. Robinson, 'Pious Pixie: Pamela Colman Smith'

stops.name: Exeter, the money runs out
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to year: financial pressure forced her from Parc Garland to Exeter in 1939 (Wikipedia). Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01. No Exeter address was found in any source consulted, so the coordinate is the city centre. The Catholic Who's Who entry for the same year still gives Parc Garland as her address; whether the directory was compiled before the move is not established.
stops.campa: The money runs out. She and Nora Lake leave the Lizard for Exeter in 1939, the year the war starts. She is sixty-one, the inheritance that paid for twenty years at the end of England is spent, and she is a tenant again, in a city, with whatever came out of the house on the cliff. No Exeter address for her has been found, and whether the directory went to press before the move nobody has established. Her entry in the Catholic Who's Who for that same year still gives her address as Parc Garland, The Lizard, Cornwall.
suggested_refs: The Catholic Who's Who, 1939, entry for Pamela Colman Smith

stops.name: Bude, Cornwall: paying in pictures
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the move to Bude in the 1940s (Wikipedia); no month or year within the decade is recorded, and 1942 is an ordering choice. The errand-boy anecdote is oral evidence reaching print through late recollection, as artcornwall itself cautions, and is [R]. Coordinate is the Bude town pin, not a residence.
stops.campa: She and Lake move to Bude on the north coast. She is known there as an artist, and remembered by at least one errand boy as a woman who sometimes paid in pictures instead of coins, which is either generosity or the plain arithmetic of having no coins. She is in her sixties, drawing something, selling nothing that anyone recorded, in a seaside town in wartime. The testimony reaches print half a century later, filtered through an old man's memory of a childhood errand.
suggested_refs: Local Bude recollections of Smith in the 1940s, collected in Dawn G. Robinson's account
sources: artcornwall.org, Dawn G. Robinson, 'Pious Pixie: Pamela Colman Smith'

stops.name: New York, the visit to the Coles
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to place and date, [A] as to the words. Kaplan prints the painter Alphaeus Cole's recollection of a visit by Smith to him and his wife Peggy in New York City, 'probably shortly after the end of World War II'. No transatlantic crossing by Smith in the 1940s is documented anywhere consulted, and she was then living in reduced circumstances in Bude, so the recollection may misplace an earlier visit in time. The date 1945-01-01 orders the stop and asserts nothing. Corrected from the research pool, which had this quotation as an incomplete line from an unlocated letter describing the Roman Catholic Church; it is neither a letter nor about the Church, but a spoken remark about being a Catholic.
stops.campa: The painter Alphaeus Cole and his wife Peggy receive a visit from her in New York, and Cole remembers one thing she said: she asks Peggy why she does not become a Catholic, and gives her reason. She is thirty-five years a convert by then, in her late sixties, and broke. Cole puts the visit shortly after the war, but no crossing of hers in the 1940s is recorded anywhere consulted, and she was living in Bude on almost nothing. The recollection may be putting an earlier visit in the wrong decade. What he is sure of is the sentence.
stops.quote: Why don't you become a Catholic, Peggy? It's such fun.
stops.quote_source: Pamela Colman Smith to Peggy Cole, New York City, c. 1945-46, as recalled by Alphaeus Cole and printed in Kaplan, Encyclopedia of Tarot III

segments.name: The Unmarked Grave and the Afterlives

stops.name: 2 Bencoolen House, Bude: the death
stops.date_confidence: 18 September 1951, per Kaplan: 'Pamela Colman Smith died at age 73 on September 18, 1951, at 2 Bencoolen House in Bude. Present at the time of her death was Mrs. Elsie T. Bates, a friend who occasionally cleaned her flat.' Contradiction flagged: Wikipedia's infobox and lead give 16 September, while its own body text, citing Kaplan, gives 18 September; the 18th is followed. Cause: 'heart disease' overstates the record. Kaplan notes only that she seems to have had some heart problems, citing a February 1939 letter sympathising that she was feeling poorly with her heart. Coordinate corrected to OSM 'Bencoolen Inn, Bencoolen Road, Bude'; the pool's figure sat 370 m north-west.
stops.campa: She dies at 2 Bencoolen House in Bude on the eighteenth of September, aged seventy-three. No cause is recorded; Kaplan says only that she seems to have had some trouble with her heart. Present is Mrs Elsie T. Bates, a friend who sometimes cleaned the flat. The building is named after a wreck and is a pub now, with ghost stories attached to it, none of them about her. She dies in debt, in rented rooms, at the other end of the county from the house she had to give up, and the deck she drew in six months forty-two years earlier is in print in two countries that month.
suggested_refs: Bencoolen House, Bude, later the Bencoolen Inn, named for the wreck of the Bencoolen
sources: artcornwall.org, Dawn G. Robinson, 'Pious Pixie: Pamela Colman Smith'

stops.name: Bude, the burial and the sale of the effects
stops.date_confidence: The burial date is unrecorded; the stop carries the date of death only to order it immediately after. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: Kaplan, the source Wikipedia itself cites, has 'a record of her burial at the local Catholic cemetery in Bude, but her grave site remains unknown', while Wikipedia paraphrases this as St Michael's Cemetery and artcornwall names St Michael and All Angels, which is Bude's Anglican parish church and sits oddly with a Catholic burial for a devout convert. Coordinate is unverifiable: no church of that name resolves in Nominatim at Bude. The debt, the auction, and Nora Lake's position are attested by artcornwall; the further claim that the auction destroyed the tarot originals is speculative and is not carried, since their whereabouts were already unrecorded before her death.
stops.campa: She is buried in Bude in a grave nobody can now find. The plot record burned before the parish books were centralised at Truro. The sources do not agree on which ground she is even in: Kaplan has a record of burial in the town's Catholic cemetery, while Wikipedia and the local accounts name St Michael's, which is the Anglican parish church. Her effects are auctioned to satisfy creditors. Nora Lake, named as beneficiary, receives substantially nothing.
suggested_refs: The 2017 'Tarot Magic in Merlin's Britain' commemorative visit, some two dozen people led by Mary K. Greer, which attempted to locate the grave by dowsing and settled on a spot at the edge of the older churchyard; a further dowsing visit in 2018 reported the same spot. Cited as reception history, not as evidence of the plot.
sources: artcornwall.org, Dawn G. Robinson, 'Pious Pixie: Pamela Colman Smith'

It goes out as Rider Tarot and as Rider Waite Tarot. The company's copyright claim covers only what the company added: the design on the backs, and the box they come in. The seventy-eight pictures inside are in the public domain and free for anyone in the United States to print. She has been dead twenty years.
suggested_refs: U.S. Games Systems editions from 1971, and the limits of their copyright claim

stops.campa: A hundred years after she drew them, U.S. Games issues a centennial edition and prints the names on it in the other order: Smith-Waite. The publisher's name comes off the front altogether, the author's goes second, the artist's goes first. It is a change to a box, made by the company that sells the box, and it settles nothing about who owned what. The cards inside are reproduced from an early printing, because the plates burned in the war and her drawings have never been found.
